title: Proxy
summary: Put a stand-in in front of an object to control access, laziness, or remote calls.

parts.rule: Proxy implements the same interface as a real subject and controls access to it. Variants include virtual proxies (lazy create), protection proxies (authz checks), and remote proxies (network stub). The client thinks it talks to the real object.
parts.why: Clients should not scatter lazy-init, permission checks, or RPC plumbing. Proxy localizes those concerns. Confusion with decorator is common: decorator adds behavior; proxy controls access to the same core behavior.

Protection: DocumentsProxy.view(user) checks ACL before calling RealDocument.view. Remote: ShippingPortProxy.serialize requests over HTTP to a shipping service implementing the same ShippingPort interface your domain already uses. body:
Rule. Proxy implements the same interface as a real subject and controls access to it. Variants include virtual proxies (lazy create), protection proxies (authz checks), and remote proxies (network stub). The client thinks it talks to the real object.

Why it matters. Clients should not scatter lazy-init, permission checks, or RPC plumbing. Proxy localizes those concerns. Confusion with decorator is common: decorator adds behavior; proxy controls access to the same core behavior.

Worked example. Image interface with display(). HighResImage loads a 20 MB file. ImageProxy holds a path; first display() loads HighResImage then forwards; later calls reuse it. Protection: DocumentsProxy.view(user) checks ACL before calling RealDocument.view. Remote: ShippingPortProxy.serialize requests over HTTP to a shipping service implementing the same ShippingPort interface your domain already uses. Client code keeps calling display or view without knowing about files, ACL tables, or sockets.  Walk one concrete path with numbers before generalizing. Keep the tone focused and honest. [[diagram:proxy]]

When to use. Use proxy for lazy loading of heavy objects, access control, and remote service stubs that match a local interface. Use it when control must be transparent to callers.

When to refuse. Refuse a proxy that changes semantics so much callers must know it is fake. Refuse proxy when decorator (adding responsibilities) is the real intent. Refuse deep proxy chains that obscure failures. Refuse remote proxies without timeouts and error mapping.
